explanations.explanation: It appears that this feature is signaling a morpheme‐boundary or clitic/affix “decision” – it helps the model decide to generate an attached suffix (like the possessive/plural “s”, ordinal endings “nd”, “th”, etc.) rather than “merging” into a longer word (which then erroneously yields something like “iginally”). In short, the feature represents an internal signal for when a short bound morpheme (an “’s”–type affix) should be produced.

It detects when a word is ending with an agentive (or related nominal) morpheme—essentially the “‑er/‑ers” ending that turns a stem into a noun denoting an actor or agent. In other words, the feature picks up on that common suffix pattern used to form agent nouns or similar derivations.

It appears this feature is detecting a suffix‐morpheme—namely the “‑ia” ending—that shows up in proper names (whether drugs, places, organizations, or brands). In context, it cues the model to complete a word with that “‑ia” ending, helping correctly form names and similar tokens.

It appears this feature is detecting when the context leads into an infinitive or purpose clause—that is, a cue from the preceding word that signals an upcoming “to” introducing a goal, instruction, or reason.

This feature appears to signal when the model is “in‐the middle” of a word—i.e. it detects portions of words (morphemes or subword segments) that need to be completed. In contexts where a token is only a part (like “Rob” in “Robot” or “onstr” in “Demonstrate”), the feature is highly active and leads the model to predict the appropriate completion (e.g. “ot”, “ate”, “ater”, etc.). Essentially, it represents a word‐completion or subword‐segmentation signal.

It appears that this feature signals a non‐default, morpheme‐specific word ending—in other words, it marks subword segments (often at the end of compound or inflected words) so that the model predicts the proper inflection (like “es”, “te”, “ies”, etc.) instead of the usual “ly” continuation.

It detects when text is formatted as structured, colon‐delimited temporal or date/time data—such as office hours, published timestamps, or schedule entries—signaling that a numerical time or date field is being listed.

It appears that this feature “fires” in contexts where the text is structured to introduce a specific, formal‐styled entity – often a proper noun, title, or a hyphenated code – whose very next token begins with an uppercase “A.” In other words, the feature is detecting a formatting or discourse “boundary” cue that signals the upcoming start of an “A–word” (as in brand names, addresses, or titles), and when it’s removed the model no longer expects that typical “A” but instead predicts punctuation or another continuation.

It appears to be a detector for “structured entity‐chunks” – that is, it flags the distinctive, semi-formatted strings (often combining numbers, abbreviations, punctuation, and foreign or proper‐name tokens) used in things like product labels, specifications, phone numbers, legal citations, etc. This feature “lights up” when the model is processing a piece of text that is formatted as a specialized, composite identifier or measurement rather than ordinary running text.

It appears to be a unit‐detection signal that “marks” the end of a multi‐token, structured entity (such as a proper name, date, title, or list element) so that the model then favors the expected continuation (e.g. a linking “and”) that unites items in a sequence.

explanations.explanation: It’s a signal that a hyphen‐like connector is present—i.e. the feature “fires” when a dash (or hyphen) is used to join parts of a compound word, number/date, or phrase, thereby biasing next‐token predictions to continue that compound construction.

It appears that the feature “fires” on the final, content‐defining token in multi‐token, structured phrases—whether that be a measurement unit (like “kg” or “ps”), a numeric label or identifier (such as “45” or “250”), or the head of a title or name (like “Pros”, “Officer”, “Father”, “Leader”). In short, the feature is capturing the “end‐marker” (or head) of a composite expression where that token signals that the phrase is complete and thereby cues the model’s continuation (often punctuation or a fixed following phrase).

This feature seems to be “lighting up” on tokens that end a phrase—often a numeral, time‐value fragment, or proper‐name subword—that cues the common follow‐up preposition “on.” In other words, it marks boundaries in formatted, structured text (like dates/times, event announcements, or UI commands) where an “on” phrase (indicating time, location, or a contextual link) is expected.

It seems that this feature is “lighting up” on language that signals a call‐to‐action or a persuasive—almost commercial—shift in tone. In other words, when the model is promoting a service, promising help, or decisively stating that something “always” happens, this feature is active; it pushes the continuation in a way that fits a sales or announcement pitch. Removing the feature causes the next-token distribution to jump to odd defaults (like “Q” or “A”), which further suggests that it normally steers the output toward the well‐formed, promotional phrasing typical of marketing language.

The feature appears to signal abbreviated tokens—markers within structured abbreviations (like a.m./p.m., initials in place or professional names such as “L.A.,” “D.C.,” “M.D.,” etc.)—guiding the model on how to parse and predict following punctuation and token boundaries in such contexts.

This feature appears to signal that the current token is the “first half” of a tightly bound multi‐token phrase (such as a compound proper noun, date range, or fixed expression), priming the model to complete that structured unit in a predictable way.

It appears to be a “glue‐or compound‐marker” signal—that is, a learned feature that flags when a punctuation (usually a hyphen or dash) isn’t meant to stand alone but bind parts of a compound or formatted string (such as dates, phone numbers, compound adjectives, or hyphenated terms) so that the following token is predicted as part of an integrated unit rather than as an isolated punctuation mark.
It's detecting the “posted” marker in timestamped entry metadata—in other words, a signal that marks a blog/forum post or similar publication announcement in structured entry text.

It appears that this feature “lights up” when the text is in a highly formalized, branded or boilerplate style—that is, when the language consists of institutional names, trademarks/copyright marks, or advertisement‐style/formatted business information. In these cases the feature shifts the model’s continuation (using words like “to” or “the” rather than a numerical placeholder) because it signals a particular style and context (for example, a corporate/legal or product–listing passage) that has its own conventional punctuation and token patterns.

This feature activates on degree‐modifying or approximation tokens—words like “Much” and “Almost”—that signal comparative or nearly quantified statements and guide the model toward agreeing with ensuing numerical or descriptive content.
